lectures.title: The `host` command & DNS Records Types: A, AAAA, CNAME, MX and NS

cues.en: Let's now have a look at DNS and the different types of records that we got there.
So there are a lot of records there, but let's have a look at the most common DNS record types.
The most one of the most common one is A that maps a domain name to an IP version four address.
Those are the normal IP addresses that we've looked at so far.
Then we also got the RR records.
Those map a domain name to an IPV six address IPV six.
We'll have a look at those in a later lecture.
And then we also got see name.
They just mean that this is an alias for another domain name.
And that one we would then of course have to resolve.
Then we can also have an MX record that specifies mail servers for a domain.
So for example, we could say, okay, here, google.com if we want to connect to that server, this
is the IP.
But if you want to send an email to that server, then there's another server.
So the way it works is that you would tell your email provider to send an email and then if that email
ends at Google.com, then your email provider would look at the MX record of Google.com and then connect
to that server.
So the idea is that the website can be operated by different servers that the email server and this
is really convenient because this allows you to, for example, outsource your emails to another provider
or to another server.
There's also another entry here that's the NS record.
They list the authoritative name servers for a domain.
So this would be important, for example, if we wanted to connect to those then later.
So this is also an important information.
We are able to list the received DNS entries with the following command.
We can just use the host command or host minus A and then to list all the available entries.
So for example, this one would list all the available DNS entries or records for Google.com.
Let's have a look at this so I can just say host Minus a google.com.
Let me zoom in a little bit and here we can now see it has connected here, we can see here, those
are all the records.
So for example, here for me right now, this is an, a record here for the IPv4 address of Google.com.
This would be the IPV six address.
Then we can also see here their name servers here provided here.
Those are not a sub domain.
They are a full domain.
That's why they end with a dot here.
Otherwise they would be a sub domain.
A sub domain would for example be w ww dot google.com or mail.google.com.
So those this mail or w ww would consider a sub domain.
But this is a complete domain because it ends with a dot.
Here we can also see different types of records here.
So for example txt they allow us to just add text data here.
This can be used, for example, to verify the domains here.
For example, this is for Apple, probably for the App store and this is probably for the Google store
to verify that they which account this domain belongs to.
Or here we can see the MX records for sending emails to at Google.com.
So we can see all of that here.
So you can see here those records, they work and, and yeah, our browser can now just look here and
it knows which IP to connect to.
It has changed now, by the way, because I've refreshed that that output and every time I refresh it,
it's telling me or quite often here it's telling me a different IP aside from the caching.
The reason is that there's this is load balancing on that side because if all people would connect to
the same IP, that would overload the server.
So the idea is if this IP always changes or it frequently changes, at least then people connect to
different IPS here.
And this helps with load balancing on the side of Google of this company.
But yeah, those are the DNS entries.
And now I want to present you with a small bonus because I want to show you by hand how we could manually
resolve the DNS entries.
The idea here is that by doing this once by hand, this gives us a deeper understanding of how the whole
DNS procedure works.
So I do want to include that here as a bonus lecture in the next lecture here in my course.
